\chapter{Numbers One to Ten}
\label{ch:numbers-1-10}
\hlchaptermodality{6}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can count from one to ten in German, say why every one of those numbers is the English number's twin rather than a Latin borrowing, and use ein and eine for \textquotedblleft{}a\textquotedblright{}.}

German's numbers are the one place the language is closer to English than any Romance language gets: they were never borrowed from Latin, they are German's own inherited words, and they are the near-twins of one to ten. This chapter teaches them one at a time, with the sound law that explains every difference between drei and three and between zehn and ten, and it collects each five into a run so that counting is one motion rather than ten remembered words. It closes with the article ein / eine, which is eins with its counting -s taken off exactly as English a and an are one worn down, and with the seam between words a language keeps and words it buys: the numbers are homegrown, the month names are Latin.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[eins]{eins — \textquotedblleft{}one,\textquotedblright{} and the German \emph{ei}}

\label{lesson:GE-C06-eins}



\begin{quote}
Here is where German is closer to English than any Romance language gets. Its numbers are not borrowed from Latin — they are German's own, and they are the near-twins of the English ones. Start with the first.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: eins}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{eins} — \textquotedblleft{}one,\textquotedblright{} the number you say when you are counting.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{diphthong-ei} — German \textbf{ei} is the English word \textbf{eye}. Always, in every word, with no exceptions to remember.
\end{itemize}

So \emph{eins} is \emph{eyns}. You already own this one: \emph{heißen} is \emph{HY-ssen}, and \emph{Wiedersehen} has an \emph{ie}, which is the other way round and says \emph{ee}. \textbf{ei} says \emph{eye}; \textbf{ie} says \emph{ee}. The second letter tells you which.
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{eins} is English \textbf{one}. Not borrowed from it, not similar to it — the same inherited word, which is why it needs no story to make it stick.

English hides the relationship in its spelling. \emph{One} is written as though it rhymed with \emph{bone}, and it did once; the \emph{w}-sound at the front (\emph{wun}) crept in later. Strip that off and \emph{one} and \emph{ein} are the same shape.

The same word is also sitting inside English \textbf{a} and \textbf{an} — \emph{an apple} is \emph{one apple}, worn down. German does exactly the same thing with \emph{eins}, and once the first five are learned there is a lesson on it.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}eins\textquotedblright{} — \emph{eyns}, with the English word \emph{eye} inside it
  \item \textquotedblleft{}eins\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}one\textquotedblright{} — the same old word
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ei\textquotedblright{} as \emph{eye}, \textquotedblleft{}ie\textquotedblright{} as \emph{ee} — the second letter decides
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \textquotedblleft{}one\textquotedblright{} in German? (\emph{Eins}.) How is \textbf{ei} said? (Like the English word \emph{eye}.) And \textbf{ie}? (\emph{Ee}.) Which English word is \emph{eins}? (\emph{One} — and \emph{a}/\emph{an} underneath it.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[zwei]{zwei — \textquotedblleft{}two,\textquotedblright{} and the \emph{z} that is a \emph{ts}}

\label{lesson:GE-C06-zwei}



\begin{quote}
One down. The second number has the same \emph{ei} you just learned, and one letter that does not say what an English reader expects.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: zwei}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{zwei} — \textquotedblleft{}two.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Said \emph{tsvy}. The \textbf{z} is the \emph{ts} of English \emph{cats} — never the buzz of English \emph{zoo}. That is the whole of the German \textbf{z}: it has one job and it never does anything else.

The other two letters you already own. The \textbf{w} is a \emph{v}, as in \emph{wohnen}, and the \textbf{ei} is \emph{eye}, as in \emph{eins}. So \emph{zwei} is three rules you have and one that is new.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{zwei} is English \textbf{two}, with the \emph{tw-} opening turned into \emph{zw-}.

English still says the \emph{tw-} out loud in the words \emph{two} grew from — \textbf{twin} (two born together), \textbf{between} (in the space of two), \textbf{twice}, \textbf{twenty}. It only lost the \emph{w} in the number itself, which is why \emph{two} is spelt with a letter nobody pronounces. German kept the pair and shifted the \emph{t} to \emph{ts}:

\begin{quote}
\emph{tw-} $\to$ \emph{zw-}: \textbf{two} / \emph{zwei}, \textbf{twin} / \emph{Zwilling}, \textbf{twelve} / \emph{zwölf}
\end{quote}

So the silent \emph{w} in English \textbf{two} is not a spelling accident. It is the \emph{w} that German still says.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}zwei\textquotedblright{} — \emph{tsvy}, the \emph{z} like the end of \emph{cats}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}eins, zwei\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}two\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}twin\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}between\textquotedblright{} — then \textquotedblleft{}zwei\textquotedblright{}, and hear the \emph{w} come back
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \textquotedblleft{}two\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{Zwei}.) How is German \textbf{z} said? (\emph{Ts}, as in \emph{cats}.) Which English words still say the \emph{w} that \emph{two} dropped? (\emph{Twin}, \emph{between}, \emph{twice}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[drei]{drei — \textquotedblleft{}three,\textquotedblright{} and German's missing \emph{th}}

\label{lesson:GE-C06-drei}



\begin{quote}
Third number, third \emph{ei}. And it shows you something that will keep paying: German has no \textbf{th} sound at all, and you can predict what it uses instead.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: drei}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{drei} — \textquotedblleft{}three.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Said \emph{dry}: the scraped \emph{r} you met in \emph{lernen}, and the \emph{ei} saying \emph{eye}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{drei} is English \textbf{three}. German simply has no \emph{th}, and where English says one, German says \textbf{d}. That is not a fact about numbers — it is a fact about the whole language, and you have been using it since your first \emph{danke}:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{English} & \textbf{German} \\
\midrule
\textbf{th}ree & \textbf{d}rei \\
\textbf{th}e & \textbf{d}er, \textbf{d}ie, \textbf{d}as \\
\textbf{th}ank & \textbf{d}anke \\
\textbf{th}at & \textbf{d}as \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Five words, one swap. Whenever an English word starts with \emph{th}, try a \emph{d} and you will often land on the German.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}drei\textquotedblright{} — \emph{dry}, scrape the \emph{r}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}eins, zwei, drei\textquotedblright{}
  \item the swap — \textquotedblleft{}three/drei\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}the/der\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}thank/danke\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \textquotedblleft{}three\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{Drei}.) What does German use where English has \textbf{th}? (\textbf{D}.) Give three pairs. (\emph{Three/drei}, \emph{the/der}, \emph{thank/danke}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(siblings, not borrowings)]{Siblings, not borrowings}

\label{lesson:GE-C06-grimm}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Drei}, \emph{three}, and Latin \emph{tres} all mean three and all start with a different sound. Before the next seven numbers, it is worth knowing why — because the answer makes each of them cheaper to learn.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: siblings and cousins}]
German and English are \textbf{siblings}. Latin is a \textbf{cousin}.

That is not a figure of speech. All three grew out of one older language, and Germanic — the parent of English and German — split off from the rest first. So \emph{drei} did not come \textbf{from} \emph{tres}, and English \emph{three} did not either. All three are what one prehistoric word became along three different roads.

Which is why the German numbers are the easy ones and the Romance numbers are the hard ones, for an English speaker: \emph{three} and \emph{drei} are the same word two doors apart, while \emph{tres} is the same word across the street.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
The differences are not random. A \textbf{sound law} is a change that happened to \emph{every} word in a language at once, so once you know one you can predict the rest.

You have already met one of these. \emph{Gut} is \emph{good} with the \textbf{d} turned to a \textbf{t}, and \emph{machen} is \emph{make} with the \textbf{k} turned to a \textbf{ch} — one shift, two words, and it caught every word in German that had those sounds.

The shift that separates Germanic from Latin is older and works the same way. The two turns worth carrying into the next lessons are:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Older sound} & \textbf{Germanic sound} & \textbf{Seen in} \\
\midrule
\textbf{t} & \textbf{th}, and German \textbf{d} & Latin \emph{tres}, English \emph{three}, German \emph{drei} \\
\textbf{p} & \textbf{f} & Latin \emph{pes} \textquotedblleft{}foot\textquotedblright{}, English \emph{foot} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

So when a Latin word and a German one sound nothing alike, try the first consonant before deciding they are unrelated. Often they are the same word, one law apart.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}tres\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}three\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}drei\textquotedblright{} — one word, three roads
  \item the two turns — \textquotedblleft{}t becomes th\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}p becomes f\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}good/gut\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}make/machen\textquotedblright{} — the shift you already knew
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is \emph{drei} borrowed from Latin \emph{tres}? (No — they are cousins, both from one older word.) What is a sound law? (A change that hit every word in the language at once, so it is predictable.) Which two turns should you carry forward? (Old \textbf{t} to \textbf{th}/\textbf{d}, old \textbf{p} to \textbf{f}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vier]{vier — \textquotedblleft{}four,\textquotedblright{} written with a \emph{v} and said with an \emph{f}}

\label{lesson:GE-C06-vier}



\begin{quote}
The fourth number is the easiest one yet — as long as you do not trust the first letter.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: vier}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{vier} — \textquotedblleft{}four.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{v-as-f} — German \textbf{v} is said as an \textbf{f}. It is not a \emph{v} sound; that job belongs to \textbf{w}.
  \item \texttt{ie-long-ee} — \textbf{ie} is a long \emph{ee}, the mirror of \textbf{ei}.
\end{itemize}

So \emph{vier} is \emph{feer}. Put the two vowel rules side by side and the pair is settled for good:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Spelling} & \textbf{Sound} & \textbf{Example} \\
\midrule
\textbf{ei} & \emph{eye} & \emph{eins}, \emph{zwei}, \emph{drei} \\
\textbf{ie} & \emph{ee} & \emph{vier}, \emph{wieder} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Both times, \textbf{the second letter is the one you say}.
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{vier} is English \textbf{four}, and once you know the \emph{v} is an \emph{f} you can hear it: \emph{feer}, \emph{four}. Latin's cousin is \emph{quattuor}, which is where Spanish \emph{cuatro} and French \emph{quatre} come from — so this is a number where English sides with German and not with the Romance languages at all.

The \emph{v}-said-as-\emph{f} is not special to this word. German writes \textbf{v} in a handful of its oldest words — \emph{vier}, \emph{Vater}, \emph{von}, \emph{voll} — and says every one of them with an \emph{f}, which is exactly the letter English uses in \emph{four}, \emph{father}, \emph{from}, \emph{full}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}vier\textquotedblright{} — \emph{feer}, the \emph{v} said as an \emph{f}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}eins, zwei, drei, vier\textquotedblright{}
  \item the vowel pair — \textquotedblleft{}ei\textquotedblright{} as \emph{eye}, \textquotedblleft{}ie\textquotedblright{} as \emph{ee}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \textquotedblleft{}four\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{Vier}, said \emph{feer}.) How is German \textbf{v} said? (As an \emph{f}.) Which letter carries the \emph{v} sound instead? (\textbf{W}.) And how do you tell \textbf{ei} from \textbf{ie}? (Say the second letter.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[fünf]{fünf — \textquotedblleft{}five,\textquotedblright{} and the law you can hear}

\label{lesson:GE-C06-fuenf}



\begin{quote}
The fifth number closes the first hand — and it is the clearest example of a sound law anywhere in the language.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: fünf}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{fünf} — \textquotedblleft{}five.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{umlaut-ue} — \textbf{ü} is an \emph{ee} said with your lips rounded for an \emph{oo}. Say \emph{ee}, hold the tongue exactly where it is, and push your lips forward.
\end{itemize}

So \emph{fünf} is roughly \emph{fewnf}, in one syllable. This is the umlaut doing what you learned it does: it takes the back vowel \textbf{u} and drags it to the front of the mouth.
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{fünf} is English \textbf{five}, and the two of them are the sound law from the last lesson caught in the act.

The older word for five began with a \textbf{p}. Latin kept it — \emph{quinque} still has one in the middle — and Germanic turned every one of those \textbf{p}s into an \textbf{f}. So English got \emph{five} and German got \emph{fünf}, both starting with the letter that was once a \emph{p}:

\begin{quote}
old \textbf{p} $\to$ Germanic \textbf{f}: \textbf{f}ive / \emph{f}ünf, against Latin's \emph{quinque}
\end{quote}

Say \emph{fünf} and \emph{five} one after the other. They are the same word, and the whole distance between them and the Latin one is that single turn.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}fünf\textquotedblright{} — say \emph{ee}, then round your lips without moving your tongue
  \item \textquotedblleft{}fünf\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}five\textquotedblright{} — one word, one law apart
  \item \textquotedblleft{}eins, zwei, drei, vier, fünf\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \textquotedblleft{}five\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{Fünf}.) How do you make \textbf{ü}? (Say \emph{ee} and round your lips.) Which sound turned into the \textbf{f} of \emph{five} and \emph{fünf}? (An older \textbf{p} — the one Latin kept.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{eins bis fünf — counting to five}

\label{lesson:GE-C06-zahlen-1-5}



\begin{quote}
Five words, one at a time. Counting is something else: it is the five of them running together without a pause to think. That is what this lesson is for, and nothing in it is new.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: the run}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{eins, zwei, drei, vier, fünf}
\end{quote}

Said straight through: \emph{eyns, tsvy, dry, feer, fewnf}.

Every one is the English number with a German coat on:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{German} & \textbf{English} & \textbf{What changed} \\
\midrule
\emph{eins} & one & nothing — English hid it in the spelling \\
\emph{zwei} & two & the \emph{tw-} German still says \\
\emph{drei} & three & \textbf{th} flattened to \textbf{d} \\
\emph{vier} & four & the \textbf{v} is said as an \textbf{f} \\
\emph{fünf} & five & an older \textbf{p}, now an \textbf{f} in both \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Not one of them is borrowed from Latin. All five are what an English speaker already half knows.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}eins, zwei, drei, vier, fünf\textquotedblright{} — straight through, no gaps
  \item it again, faster
  \item it backwards — \textquotedblleft{}fünf, vier, drei, zwei, eins\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}eins, zwei, drei, vier, fünf\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Count to five. (\emph{Eins, zwei, drei, vier, fünf}.) Now backwards. (\emph{Fünf, vier, drei, zwei, eins}.) Which of the five is borrowed from Latin? (None of them.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ein / eine]{ein und eine — when \textquotedblleft{}one\textquotedblright{} becomes \textquotedblleft{}a\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C06-ein-eine}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Eins} is what you say while counting. Put it in front of a naming word and it changes shape — and English does the very same trick, so this costs almost nothing.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: ein / eine}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{ein} / \textbf{eine} — \textquotedblleft{}a,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}an,\textquotedblright{} and also \textquotedblleft{}one\textquotedblright{} when it sits in front of a naming word.
\end{quote}

Which of the two you use follows the same three-way split you already know from \emph{der}, \emph{die}, \emph{das}:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{The word takes} & \textbf{So \textquotedblleft{}a\textquotedblright{} is} \\
\midrule
\emph{der} & \textbf{ein} \\
\emph{das} & \textbf{ein} \\
\emph{die} & \textbf{eine} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Two of the three groups share one form, so there is really only one thing to remember: \textbf{die} words take the extra \textbf{-e}. On the two nouns inside \emph{guten Tag} and \emph{gute Nacht}:

\begin{quote}
\emph{der Tag} $\to$ \textbf{ein Tag}, \textquotedblleft{}a day\textquotedblright{} · \emph{die Nacht} $\to$ \textbf{eine Nacht}, \textquotedblleft{}a night\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the counting -s drops}]
\textbf{Counting form: \emph{eins}. In front of a naming word: \emph{ein} / \emph{eine}.} The \emph{-s} belongs to counting and to nothing else.

English does the identical thing, and hides it just as well. \emph{One} in front of a naming word wore down to \textbf{a} and \textbf{an} — \emph{an apple} really is \emph{one apple}, said quickly for a thousand years. So both languages have a special worn-down shape of \textquotedblleft{}one\textquotedblright{}, and both use it as the word for \textquotedblleft{}a\textquotedblright{}.

The other numbers do not do this. \emph{Zwei}, \emph{drei}, \emph{vier} and \emph{fünf} look exactly the same whether you are counting or putting them in front of something. Only the first number has two shapes, in German as in English.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}eins\textquotedblright{} — then \textquotedblleft{}ein\textquotedblright{}, dropping the \emph{s}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}der Tag / ein Tag\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}die Nacht / eine Nacht\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}one apple\textquotedblright{}, then \textquotedblleft{}an apple\textquotedblright{} — English doing the same thing
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What happens to \emph{eins} in front of a naming word? (It drops the \emph{-s}: \emph{ein}.) Which group takes \emph{eine}? (The \emph{die} group.) Which English words are the same worn-down \textquotedblleft{}one\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{A} and \emph{an}.) Do the other numbers change? (No — only the first.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sechs]{sechs — \textquotedblleft{}six,\textquotedblright{} where \emph{chs} is just an \emph{x}}

\label{lesson:GE-C06-sechs}



\begin{quote}
The second hand starts here. And the sixth number quietly settles the last thing German \textbf{ch} can do.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: sechs}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{sechs} — \textquotedblleft{}six.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{ch-none} — in \textbf{chs}, the \emph{ch} makes no throat sound at all. The pair is a plain \textbf{ks}, exactly the English letter \emph{x}.
\end{itemize}

So \emph{sechs} is \emph{zeks}, and it rhymes with English \emph{sex} — which is also, as it happens, the Latin word for six.

That completes the \textbf{ch}: raspy after \emph{a} as in \emph{machen}, and silent-into-\emph{ks} when an \emph{s} follows. Nothing else to learn about it.
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{sechs} is English \textbf{six}, and here the two languages have barely moved apart at all — \emph{zeks} against \emph{siks}. Even the Latin cousin \emph{sex} is close enough to hear, because this is one of the few numbers no sound law rearranged much.

Which makes it the cheapest number in the chapter: if you can say \emph{x}, you can say \emph{sechs}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}sechs\textquotedblright{} — \emph{zeks}, no throat rasp
  \item \textquotedblleft{}machen\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}sechs\textquotedblright{} — the two jobs of \emph{ch}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}sechs\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}six\textquotedblright{} — barely a step apart
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \textquotedblleft{}six\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{Sechs}, said \emph{zeks}.) What does \textbf{ch} do in front of an \emph{s}? (Nothing — the pair is a plain \emph{ks}.) And after an \emph{a}? (The raspy throat sound, as in \emph{machen}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sieben]{sieben — \textquotedblleft{}seven,\textquotedblright{} and the buzzing \emph{s}}

\label{lesson:GE-C06-sieben}



\begin{quote}
You have been saying \emph{sechs} as \emph{zeks} without being told why. Here is the rule, on the number that needs it most.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: sieben}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{sieben} — \textquotedblleft{}seven.\textquotedblright{} Two syllables: \emph{ZEE-ben}.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{s-voiced} — a German \textbf{s} in front of a vowel \textbf{buzzes}, like the English letter \emph{z}. At the end of a word it goes back to a plain hiss.
  \item \texttt{ie-long-ee} — the long \emph{ee} again, as in \emph{vier}.
\end{itemize}

So \emph{sieben} is \emph{ZEE-ben}, not \emph{SEE-ben}. And it explains the two numbers before it: \emph{sechs} is \emph{zeks} and not \emph{seks} for the same reason.
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{sieben} is English \textbf{seven}, with the middle consonant softened from a \emph{v} to a \emph{b} — a swap those two letters make in each other's direction constantly, because they are made with the same lips.

This is the one number where the Latin cousin is also unmistakable: \emph{septem}, which English still uses in \emph{September} and in \emph{septet}. Seven is the number almost nobody's language disguised.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}sieben\textquotedblright{} — \emph{ZEE-ben}, buzz the \emph{s}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}sechs, sieben\textquotedblright{} — both start with the buzz
  \item \textquotedblleft{}sieben\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}seven\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \textquotedblleft{}seven\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{Sieben}, said \emph{ZEE-ben}.) What does a German \textbf{s} do in front of a vowel? (It buzzes, like \emph{z}.) And at the end of a word? (It hisses.) Which English word is \emph{sieben}? (\emph{Seven} — the \emph{v} softened to a \emph{b}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[acht]{acht — \textquotedblleft{}eight,\textquotedblright{} on a rasp you already have}

\label{lesson:GE-C06-acht}



\begin{quote}
Nothing new in the mouth for this one. You met its sound on the very first \emph{Gute Nacht}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: acht}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{acht} — \textquotedblleft{}eight.\textquotedblright{} Said \emph{akht}.
\end{quote}

The \textbf{ch} is the raspy back-of-the-throat sound from \emph{Nacht} and \emph{machen}: a clean open \emph{ah}, then the scrape. One syllable, no vowel after it.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{acht} is English \textbf{eight} — and the pairing is easier to believe once you notice that English still \emph{writes} the missing sound.

\emph{Eight} has a \textbf{gh} in it that nobody says. It is not decoration. English used to make a real throat scrape there, exactly the one German still makes, and the spelling is the fossil left behind after the sound fell out.

So German \textbf{-cht-} answers English \textbf{-ght-}, and it does it every single time:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{German} & \textbf{English} \\
\midrule
a\textbf{cht} & ei\textbf{ght} \\
Na\textbf{cht} & ni\textbf{ght} \\
Li\textbf{cht} & li\textbf{ght} \\
re\textbf{cht} & ri\textbf{ght} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{Nacht} and \emph{night} you already own. The pattern is worth more than the number: whenever you see a German word with \textbf{cht}, try the English one with \textbf{ght}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}acht\textquotedblright{} — \emph{akht}, open \emph{ah} then the scrape
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Nacht\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}acht\textquotedblright{} — the same ending twice
  \item the pairs — \textquotedblleft{}acht/eight\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}Nacht/night\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}Licht/light\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \textquotedblleft{}eight\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{Acht}.) What does German \textbf{-cht-} answer in English? (\textbf{-ght-}.) Why does \emph{eight} have a silent \textbf{gh}? (English used to say the same scrape German still says.) Give another pair. (\emph{Nacht}/\emph{night}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[neun]{neun — \textquotedblleft{}nine,\textquotedblright{} in the vowel of \emph{Deutsch}}

\label{lesson:GE-C06-neun}



\begin{quote}
Ninth number, and again nothing new to learn in the mouth — you got this vowel from the name of the language itself.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: neun}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{neun} — \textquotedblleft{}nine.\textquotedblright{} Said \emph{noyn}.
\end{quote}

The \textbf{eu} is the \emph{oy} of English \emph{boy}, which is exactly what it does in \emph{Deutsch}. So \emph{neun} rhymes with English \emph{coin}, and it is one syllable with an \emph{n} at each end.

Do not let the spelling talk you into \emph{new-n}. German \textbf{eu} is never two separate vowels.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{neun} is English \textbf{nine}, and the two have kept the same skeleton: \emph{n}, a vowel, \emph{n}. Only the vowel wandered — German to \emph{oy}, English to \emph{eye}.

The Latin cousin is the odd one out here. \emph{Novem} has a \emph{v} where the Germanic words have nothing, which is why Spanish \emph{nueve} and French \emph{neuf} look like a different word. Between \emph{neun} and \emph{nine} there is nothing to explain.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}neun\textquotedblright{} — \emph{noyn}, rhyming with \emph{coin}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Deutsch\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}neun\textquotedblright{} — the same \emph{eu}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}sieben, acht, neun\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \textquotedblleft{}nine\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{Neun}, said \emph{noyn}.) How is \textbf{eu} said? (Like the \emph{oy} of \emph{boy}, as in \emph{Deutsch}.) What do \emph{neun} and \emph{nine} share? (\emph{N}, a vowel, \emph{n} — only the vowel moved.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[zehn]{zehn — \textquotedblleft{}ten,\textquotedblright{} and one consonant in three photographs}

\label{lesson:GE-C06-zehn}



\begin{quote}
The last one. And it is the number that shows both of German's sound laws working, one after the other, on the same letter.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: zehn}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{zehn} — \textquotedblleft{}ten.\textquotedblright{} Said \emph{tsayn}.
\end{quote}

The \textbf{z} is the \emph{ts} you met in \emph{zwei}, and the \textbf{h} does what it did in \emph{wohnen} and \emph{gehen}: it says nothing and stretches the vowel in front of it. So: \emph{ts}, a long \emph{ay}, and an \emph{n}.

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin \emph{decem}, English \textbf{ten}, German \textbf{zehn}. One word, photographed at three moments of the same consonant walking:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Stage} & \textbf{Word} & \textbf{The sound} \\
\midrule
what Latin kept & \emph{decem} & \textbf{d} \\
the first law & \textbf{ten} & \textbf{d} became \textbf{t} \\
the second law & \emph{zehn} & \textbf{t} became \textbf{ts} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The first step is the law from the \emph{drei} lesson, the one that separated Germanic from Latin. The second is the \emph{later} shift you already know from \emph{gut} and \emph{machen} — the one that only German went through, which is why English stopped at \emph{ten} and German carried on to \emph{zehn}.

So the distance between \emph{ten} and \emph{zehn} is not a different word. It is one extra step down a road English stopped walking.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}zehn\textquotedblright{} — \emph{tsayn}, long vowel, silent \emph{h}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}decem, ten, zehn\textquotedblright{} — the same consonant, three times
  \item \textquotedblleft{}acht, neun, zehn\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \textquotedblleft{}ten\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{Zehn}, said \emph{tsayn}.) What does the \textbf{h} do? (Nothing — it lengthens the vowel.) Walk \emph{decem} to \emph{zehn}. (\emph{D} became \emph{t}, and German took the \emph{t} on to \emph{ts}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{sechs bis zehn — finishing the count}

\label{lesson:GE-C06-zahlen-6-10}



\begin{quote}
Five more words learned one at a time. Same job as before: make them one run, then join the two runs together.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: the second run}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{sechs, sieben, acht, neun, zehn}
\end{quote}

Said straight through: \emph{zeks, ZEE-ben, akht, noyn, tsayn}.

And the second five are the same story as the first — English twins, Latin only a cousin:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{German} & \textbf{English} & \textbf{What changed} \\
\midrule
\emph{sechs} & six & almost nothing; \emph{chs} is \emph{x} \\
\emph{sieben} & seven & the \emph{v} softened to a \emph{b} \\
\emph{acht} & eight & German still says the scrape English writes as \textbf{gh} \\
\emph{neun} & nine & only the vowel moved \\
\emph{zehn} & ten & an old \textbf{d} to \textbf{t}, then \textbf{t} to \textbf{ts} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}sechs, sieben, acht, neun, zehn\textquotedblright{} — straight through
  \item all ten from the start, in one breath if you can
  \item the ten backwards, from \textquotedblleft{}zehn\textquotedblright{} down to \textquotedblleft{}eins\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}eins, zwei, drei, vier, fünf, sechs, sieben, acht, neun, zehn\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Count from six to ten. (\emph{Sechs, sieben, acht, neun, zehn}.) Now all ten. Which of the ten is borrowed from Latin? (None — every one is the English number's twin.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(homegrown numbers, imported months)]{Homegrown numbers, imported months}

\label{lesson:GE-C06-monate-latein}



\begin{quote}
You have ten numbers and not one of them came from Latin. That is worth holding onto, because the very next thing German counts with \textbf{did} come from Latin — and you can hear the join.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: a language keeps some words and buys others}]
A language does not import evenly. The words people use every hour of every day are the hardest to displace, and the words that arrive with an institution come in whole.

Numbers are the first kind. German counts with its own inherited words, and so does English. Month names are the second kind: they arrived with the Roman calendar, and both languages simply took them.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
The Roman year began in \textbf{March}. Count from there and the last four months of the year land on the Latin words for seven, eight, nine and ten — which is why those four month names are numbers wearing a disguise, in German exactly as in English.

Say each Latin number and then the German one that means the same thing:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{The Latin number inside} & \textbf{German counts it} \\
\midrule
\emph{septem} — seven & \emph{sieben} \\
\emph{octo} — eight & \emph{acht} \\
\emph{novem} — nine & \emph{neun} \\
\emph{decem} — ten & \emph{zehn} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Not one pair sounds like a pair. The month names came from one language and the counting words from another, and German never reconciled them — because there was never any reason to.

You will meet the German month names themselves in a later chapter. What matters now is that when you get there, they will look Latin, and the numbers you have just learned will still be German.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}sieben, acht, neun, zehn\textquotedblright{} — the German four
  \item \textquotedblleft{}septem, octo, novem, decem\textquotedblright{} — the Latin four
  \item which kind of word a language keeps, and which it buys
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Did German borrow its numbers? (No — they are its own.) Did it borrow its month names? (Yes, from Latin, with the calendar.) Why do four of them carry the wrong number? (The Roman year began in March, so \emph{septem} was the seventh month.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — counting, and asking for one}

\label{lesson:GE-C06-practice}



\begin{quote}
Ten numbers, one article, and one fact about which words a language keeps. Put them to work.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the ten, and what each one cost}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{German} & \textbf{Said} & \textbf{English twin} \\
\midrule
\emph{eins} & \emph{eyns} & one \\
\emph{zwei} & \emph{tsvy} & two \\
\emph{drei} & \emph{dry} & three \\
\emph{vier} & \emph{feer} & four \\
\emph{fünf} & \emph{fewnf} & five \\
\emph{sechs} & \emph{zeks} & six \\
\emph{sieben} & \emph{ZEE-ben} & seven \\
\emph{acht} & \emph{akht} & eight \\
\emph{neun} & \emph{noyn} & nine \\
\emph{zehn} & \emph{tsayn} & ten \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Ten numbers and not one of them borrowed. Every one is the English word with a predictable coat on, which is the whole reason this chapter was cheap.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{The exchange}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{German} & \textbf{English} \\
\midrule
\emph{Eins, zwei, drei …} & One, two, three… \\
\emph{Und?} & And? \\
\emph{… vier, fünf, sechs, sieben, acht, neun, zehn!} & …four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten! \\
\emph{Sehr gut!} & Very good! \\
\emph{Danke!} — \emph{Bitte.} & Thanks! — You're welcome. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Every word in that exchange is one you already own, and seven of them you learned this chapter.

Then the article, on the two nouns \emph{guten Tag} and \emph{gute Nacht} are built from:

\begin{quote}
\emph{der Tag} $\to$ \textbf{ein Tag} · \emph{die Nacht} $\to$ \textbf{eine Nacht}
\end{quote}

\emph{Eins} on its own keeps its \textbf{-s}, because nothing follows it. The moment a naming word arrives, the \emph{-s} comes off.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item all ten, straight through
  \item the exchange, both voices
  \item \textquotedblleft{}eins\textquotedblright{} as a count, then \textquotedblleft{}ein\textquotedblright{} as an article — the \emph{-s} comes off
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}eins, zwei, drei, vier, fünf, sechs, sieben, acht, neun, zehn\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Count to ten. When does \emph{eins} become \emph{ein}? (In front of a naming word.) Are the German numbers borrowed from Latin? (No — they are the English numbers' twins.) Which German words \emph{were} borrowed from Latin? (The month names.)
\end{tcolorbox}
